Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here's what he thinks about the new variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Image, and more on the iPhone 18 Pro.

Stalman dives deep into the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture camera

While this year's iPhone 18 Pro brings a number of new features including a 2nm A20 Pro chip, new vapor chamber, and smaller Dynamic Island, the standout camera upgrade is undoubtedly the variable aperture system.

Also new this year are updates to Cinematic mode, Photographic Styles with new Texture controls, Apple Reference Image, and further refinements to the pro controls in the Camera app.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman shared his thoughts on all the new hardware and software features of the iPhone 18 Pro camera, as reviews continue to drop with the review embargo lifting – including our own over at 9to5Mac.

Stalman notes that while he loved last year's Cosmic Orange color of the iPhone 17 Pro, it has a tendency to reflect in images when shooting through glass. As such, he suggests that pro photographers consider Deep Blue or Black, as those colors are less likely to add unwanted color casts to your photos and videos.

He also made clear from the start that this review compares the iPhone 18 Pro camera to the iPhone 15 Pro, while the review video itself was shot almost entirely on the iPhone 17 Pro.

Talking about the key upgrade to the main lens – the new variable aperture – Stalman says this feature is "a step towards making the iPhone a real camera."

He also notes that the larger f/1.48 aperture lets more light hit the sensor, helping to keep ISO lower in low-light environments and reducing the need to trigger Night Mode.

This section of the review features some great photos of the aperture blades opening and closing, with Stalman pointing out that Apple's design is fairly unique, as the aperture blades sit on top of the main lens elements rather than being buried deep within the lens like traditional camera optical designs.

Stalman also says that the 4x zoom on iPhone 18 Pro (also found on last year's iPhone) is a significant improvement over the 5x zoom on iPhone 16 Pro, which sometimes felt a bit too tight in terms of focal length.

When it comes to features that might "go too far," he briefly touches on the new AI editing tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Re-Frame, noting that while they're technically impressive and look realistic, they alter the image so much that the final result doesn't retain the feeling of the original work.

Moving on to the new Texture options on the iPhone 18 Pro – Smooth Skin, Glow, and Film – Stalman demonstrates each one at strengths from 0 to 100. His verdict: Smooth Skin does a good job of subtly reducing skin texture without simply blurring skin; Glow delivers a diffused highlight haze similar to a professional black pro-mist filter.

He was also impressed with the grain and halation effects of the Film mode, though he wishes Apple would offer more options to let users control how much grain is applied.

The review also covers Apple Reference Image, iPhone Cinematic mode (and why Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic video), the new Apple Log 2, and includes photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro throughout.
